prayer.text: O Sacrament most holy, O Sacrament divine, all praise and all thanksgiving be every moment thine.

cues.text: A Priest at the Breaking of the Host
On the morning of July 25, 1535, around seven o'clock, Father Domenico Occelli was celebrating Mass at the main altar of the Collegiate Church of San Secondo in Asti, in northern Italy.
At the breaking of the Host, he noticed the bread turning visibly red along the entire line of the break, as though becoming living blood before his eyes.
Drops Into the Chalice
Three drops fell from the Host into the chalice below, and a fourth remained visible at its edge.
Father Domenico, uncertain at first how to proceed, continued the Mass.
When he came to break off the small portion meant for the chalice, blood again came visibly from the Host.
He could no longer doubt what he was seeing; he turned to the congregation and invited them to come forward and witness it for themselves.
A Bishop's Report and a Papal Indulgence
Bishop Scipione Roero of Asti had a notary draw up a formal act recording the event and sent his own report of it to the Holy See.
Pope Paul III responded with an Apostolic Brief dated November 6, 1535.
It granted a plenary indulgence to anyone who visited the Church of San Secondo on the miracle’s anniversary and recited three Our Fathers and three Hail Marys for the pope’s intentions.
Soldiers of an Occupying Garrison
Asti at the time lay under the dominion of Emperor Charles V, whose troops, many of them sympathetic to the new Protestant teachings then dividing Europe, were garrisoned in the city.

According to an inscription later carved in marble to commemorate the event, some of these soldiers, witnessing what had happened at the altar, were moved to abandon their heretical views and return to the Catholic faith.
Legacy
Asti's collegiate church would go on to be the site of a second reported Eucharistic sign in 1718.
The 1535 event remains the better documented of the two, anchored in a bishop's own notarized report and a papal brief issued within months of the Mass itself.
Nearly five centuries later, the account still stands as a case where soldiers stationed far from home witnessed an unexpected sign.
It came amid Europe's religious upheaval and settled, for at least some of them, a question their own age was fiercely divided over.
